I'm assuming you mean 24 hour news networks. Those came into being around the same time as voting machines. There was about a decades difference, but in the long run no one is going to notice or think anything of it.

24 hour news networks are important because they signal the end of objectivity in newscasting (I understand that actual objectivity was never achieved, but it was something that newscasters strove for).

The FCC allowed companies to broadcast television over radio waves back in the 40s and 50s so long as they devoted one hour a day to keeping the public informed via news. There were all kinds of regulations that went with this, one of the biggies being that they weren't allowed to take sides politically, and they couldn't broadcast the news for profit. That set the standard for newcasting until the early nineties when the 24 hour networks came into play. These were for profit companies, which means they required steady ad revenue, which means they had to make the news entertaining. They were also not beholden to the rules that were set for the non-profit, non-partisan news that the FCC required since they were offered on cable, and not over the radiowaves. They delegitimized the news and replaced it with punditry.
